title: US and China discuss AI safety plan ahead of Trump-Xi summit
description: Top US and Chinese officials have discussed creating a new "notification mechanism" for AI incidents that could affect national security, Treasury Sec
body: Top US and Chinese officials have discussed creating a new "notification mechanism" for AI incidents that could affect national security, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told reporters on Sunday.Bessent made the comments after what he called "successful" talks with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng in New York.The meeting came as US President Donald Trump and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping are due to hold a summit in Washington later this week.AI has come under intense scrutiny in recent days after researchers warned of the potential risks posed by the technology and some of the industry's most high profile figures called for developers to take a more cautious approach."We think that, just like with any cross-border activity, that moving from opaque to more transparency between the number one and the number two AI powers in the world is very important," Bessent told reporters after the talks.He said the meeting also covered other topics, including plans to "operationalise" a process to identify potential tariff cuts on goods called the Board of Trade.A truce in the tariffs war between the world's two biggest economies is due to expire on 10 November.The BBC has contacted the Chinese embassy in the US for comment.Chinese state news agency Xinhua said the two sides had "candid, in-depth and constructive exchanges on key economic and trade issues", noting that they had discussed AI.Bessent said in a post on X on Sunday that the talks "help lay the groundwork for President Trump to advance America's economic interests and deliver results for the American people."The US and China are locked in a race to dominate the AI and technology industries.In recent days Washington has faced calls to slow down the development of AI over fears  abouts its potential negative impact on humanity.Trump has largely dismissed those concerns, arguing that there are sufficient policies around AI and that the US cannot lose its edge to China.He said earlier this month "whoever wins in AI, wins."In May, when Xi hosted Trump in Beijing, ways to collaborate on AI was one of the issues the two leaders discussed.Those talks ended with an agreement that China would buy Boeing jets and US agricultural goods in exchange for lower tariffs.

schema.headline: US and China discuss AI safety plan ahead of Trump-Xi summit

title: Sock sensors and smart mattresses - is this the future of dementia care?
description: Image caption, Jyoti and Bharat Patel are "super testers" of dementia technology in an NHS trialByNat WrightSenior Health Producer  and Jim ReedHealth
body: Image caption, Jyoti and Bharat Patel are "super testers" of dementia technology in an NHS trialByNat WrightSenior Health Producer  and Jim ReedHealth reporterThere are sensors in every room of Jyoti and Bharat Patel's home. Their movements and habits are monitored constantly.But this doesn't worry them, in fact it gives them peace of mind.Jyoti was diagnosed with dementia five years ago, and they are now part of an NHS trial using high-tech devices to help patients live at home safely.The couple, who are in their 70s, are one of more than 250 families participating in the project by the UK Dementia Research Institute (UK DRI).The hope is that the technology could be extended more widely across the health service, to reduce preventable trips to hospital and give families peace of mind.Image source, Bharat PatelImage caption, Bharat and Jyoti travelled all over the world as professional magiciansBharat and Jyoti met at a magic show in 1977 and became a double act, with their career leading them to meet King Charles and Princess Anne as well as a host of celebrities.In 2019, Bharat started noticing that Jyoti was making uncharacteristic mistakes on stage."Normally she used to set my stage up and everything was perfect, but I saw something I was looking for and it wasn't there, so I thought something is wrong," he said.They went to a private health specialist who diagnosed Jyoti with Alzheimer's in 2021.Jyoti says when she went out, if she did not look around her, she would find that she was lost."I didn't know it [was] dementia but I knew it was something which [was] unusual," Bharat says.Image caption, The couple sleep on a smart mattress that tracks Jyoti's heart rate and breathingIn 2023, they were approached by the team at UK Dementia Research Institute and Imperial College London to take part in the trial, which is funded by the medical research charity LifeArc.Their house in west London is now fitted with different sensors, which are connected via the internet, that send data back to a dedicated team of doctors, nurses and other clinical specialists.The team then uses the information to better understand how the person is managing their daily routine, identify early signs of changing health and care needs with the hope that they can maintain independence for longer.Door sensors detect if someone leaves in the middle of the night, movement is monitored to check for signs of a fall, while kitchen appliances are fitted with sensors to check whether Jyoti has eaten and is sticking to her daily routine.The couple sleep on a "smart mattress" to track sleep disturbances and Jyoti's heart and breathing rates, which can spot early signs of an infection.Alongside this trial, Jyoti is also testing out smart socks and a special watch that also contain sensors to monitor her body temperature and keep track of any long-term changes in her gait - indicating frailty.How much will it cost and is it worth it?Costs are expected to be about £2,000 a year, mainly to cover the monitoring and paying healthcare staff to analyse the data.If rolled out more widely that could be a significant amount of money with almost a million people living with dementia in the UK.But Sarah Daniels, health and social care lead at the UK Dementia Research Institute, says the cost is no more than a couple of weeks in a care home.The main aim, she says, is to give earlier signals to health and social care professionals."Earlier signals means earlier intervention, which means we can head potential complications of an infection, potential challenges around care, we can head that off before it becomes a crisis," says Daniels.Image caption, Devices around the home pick up movement and alert care staff if neededNone of the devices record sound or video, protecting the individual's privacy, however, some people may feel nervous about the amount of data they are allowing other people to access.Daniels argues that by enhancing the level of information you provide to your GP, it enables them to make better decisions about your care.The number of people with dementia in the UK is expected to climb by another 40% by 2040, so the hope is to extend it more widely across the health service.Dr Jeremy Isaacs, national clinical director for dementia and older people's mental health at NHS England, said the health service would be closely monitoring the trial and said the research built on NHS programmes which were already supporting people to remain more independent in their own homes.While some people might feel uneasy about having all these sensors in their home, Bharat says they give him greater "peace of mind"."Even if it can cut down my worries by 5 or 10%, then it helps me and it will help other people too," he says.

schema.headline: Sock sensors and smart mattresses - is this the future of dementia care?

title: Will you get £13,000 a year when you stop working? Here's how to check
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByCost of living correspondentUpdated 36 minutes agoIt may well be decades away, but do you know how much money you will get
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByCost of living correspondentUpdated 36 minutes agoIt may well be decades away, but do you know how much money you will get when you stop working?The current state pension is soon likely to top £13,000 a year.Yet one in eight people surveyed by the UK tax authority have never checked how much money they are forecast to receive.Here's how to find out, and what you can do now to boost it.How much is the state pension?If you're working, it is highly likely you're contributing to the state pension - paid by the government when you hit pension age in your late 60s. At the moment:the flat-rate state pension - for those who reached state pension age after April 2016 - is £241.30 a week (£12,547.60 a year)the old basic state pension - for those who reached state pension age before April 2016 - is £184.90 a week (£9,614.80 a year)Many people on the old basic state pension may receive a top-up called the additional state pension. How do I qualify for it?Workers pay National Insurance (NI) contributions. In general, you need 35 years of qualifying contributions to get a full state pension.You may have gaps in your NI record if, for example, you have lived abroad. If you've taken time away from work to care for children or family members, then you get NI credits if you receive child benefit or carer's allowance.It's possible to boost your contribution history with voluntary payments. Since April 2025, you have only been able to make payments for the previous six years.That's one reason why it is important to check your state pension forecast well before you retire, experts say.How do I check what I'll get?You can see what you are forecast to receive:By downloading the HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) app, externalUsing the official online state pension forecast webpage, externalTo get a state pension, you will need to prove your identity using official photo ID.Importantly, never click on a link sent in an unsolicited email or text message, even if it looks official, as it could be a scam.For more general information about tax and pensions, HMRC has launched a Tax Confident website, external.And the government-funded, independent Money Helper website has a free retirement guidance tool, external to walk you through the options.Why haven't you checked?The most common reason for not checking a state pension forecast was feeling that retirement was still too far away to think about, a recent survey of 5,000 consumers by HMRC found.Losing track of pension pots from previous jobs, and concerns about how career breaks might affect their entitlement, were also frequent responses.People aged 45-54 were the most likely to have never checked."Whether retirement is decades away or just around the corner, I'd encourage everyone to check their forecast and see if there's anything they can do now to boost their entitlement later," says Myrtle Lloyd, HMRC's chief customer officer.

schema.headline: Will you get £13,000 a year when you stop working? Here's how to check

title: German state elections: Chancellor Friedrich Merz vows to stay on despite 'disaster' in polls
description: German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has called a local election defeat for his party, the Christian Democratic Union (CDU), a "disaster" but vowed to rem
body: German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has called a local election defeat for his party, the Christian Democratic Union (CDU), a "disaster" but vowed to remain in post.In the north-eastern state of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, the CDU fell short of a 5% threshold to enter parliament, underperforming against what had already been projected to be the party's worst ever result in the area.Far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) was on track to win the most votes in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, but it is unlikely to govern as other parties refuse to work with it.Meanwhile in Berlin, the ruling CDU was on course to be beaten by Die Linke (The Left).Merz is under mounting pressure after months of poor approval ratings, and there have been rumours he could be replaced mid-term in a so-called chancellor swap.Following the results, AfD co-leader Alice Weidel was asked by the BBC how long Merz has left in office, to which she replied, in English, "Pretty soon, he's going to leave".The two local elections took place on Sunday, a fortnight after the CDU saw its vote halved in the state of Saxony-Anhalt, where the AfD won a major victory.Echoing comments he made after that defeat, Merz told reporters at the party's Berlin headquarters on Sunday that he would forge ahead with his coalition government's plans to push through a package of economic, tax and welfare reforms."The reforms have to come," he insisted. "I am taking on this responsibility, because I want to move our country forward"."What needs to be done now requires backbone, steadfastness and patience," Merz said. "I will demonstrate this as CDU party chairman and, above all, as chancellor of our country.""I would even go so far as to say that these reforms are the antidote to the authoritarian poison that, with the fascination of authoritarianism, is penetrating ever deeper into our society," Merz added.But Weidel argues: "We are the strongest force and have reached the mainstream of the population."Some branches of the populist AfD are classed as right-wing extremist by domestic intelligence, a designation it strongly rejects.But its anti-immigration, German-first, and Russian-friendly agenda has found fertile ground in the country's former communist east.The CDU leader quickly went on the offensive, declaring that he is going nowhere.Merz has long coveted the top job in German politics, and likely won't give it up easily.Polls for both states closed at 18:00 local time (17:00 BST), with a final result expected later on Sunday night, or even Monday morning.Public broadcasters ZDF and ARD put the AfD slightly ahead in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, where the CDU has likely posted its worst result in any state since World War Two.The AfD was projected to take 38% of the vote share in the state, followed in second place by the centre-left SPD, on 35%.For Berlin, the broadcasters put the CDU on 19% of the vote share, behind Die Linke - which has never topped polls in the capital before - on nearly 26%.The AfD also looks set to increase its vote in Berlin, with a projected 16% of the vote.Prior to Sunday's elections, there had been intense speculation in Germany that Merz could be replaced unless his party's political fortunes improved.Earlier this week, the leaders of eight German states backed Merz, who has only been chancellor for 16 months.On Sunday, Burkard Dregger from the CDU in Berlin, told the BBC it was right that Merz should stay on. "He has a lot of work to do and we don't have time to waste to form new government in the federal level".

schema.headline: German state elections: Chancellor Friedrich Merz vows to stay on despite 'disaster' in polls

title: What food items should you stock up on in case of an emergency?
description: You should aim to take in about 1,500-2,500ml of fluid a day, whatever the weather, says McManamon.This can obviously come from bottled water, but als
body: You should aim to take in about 1,500-2,500ml of fluid a day, whatever the weather, says McManamon.This can obviously come from bottled water, but also from what she describes as fluid-rich tinned foods if supplies are short.For those worried about whether tinned food is as nutritious as fresh food, Dr Gill says it absolutely can be used as part of a healthy diet."There is little difference nutritionally between canned and fresh food in terms of macronutrients, like carbohydrates, protein, fats, and fibre, as well as fat-soluble vitamins, like vitamin A and E, and minerals," she says.It may not be as good for other vitamins, such as B and C, because the canning process has been found to decrease vitamin levels, but Gill offers assurances that these foods can still be a "useful source" of vitamins.

schema.headline: What food items should you stock up on in case of an emergency?

title: UK should 'team up' with Canada in new Europe alliance, Canadian minister says
description: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney's visit to address the EU in Strasbourg, shortly after von der Leyen's proposal was made, was "to build the allian
body: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney's visit to address the EU in Strasbourg, shortly after von der Leyen's proposal was made, was "to build the alliance of the future", Champagne said.Carney, the former governor of the Bank of England, has previously talked about an alliance of "middle powers" working together on economic growth, resilience and security.Champagne told the BBC that the UK and Canada had shared values."We need to look at partnership in a different way and the great thing is that when you look at Canada - and I would say the United Kingdom - we share the same values. We are very aligned in our vision of the world. Why don't we team up?" he said."We are independent and sovereign, but we are stronger together."After his return to the White House last year, US President Donald Trump imposed sweeping global tariffs, including on long-standing trade allies such as the UK.While the UK renegotiated a trade deal with the US in June last year, the new Canada-EU alliance does raise questions for the UK's post-Brexit positioning with Europe, as well as its position with the US, after some changes of presidential rhetoric over the Falklands and Irish unity in recent weeks.Carney met Prime Minister Andy Burnham in Liverpool in the middle of his trip to Brussels and Strasbourg last week, while Champagne attended a meeting of EU finance ministers in Dublin on Friday, alongside Chancellor John Healey.The developing discussions around closer ties between the EU and Canada come as Ottawa remains locked in an escalating trade war with the US, with both sides imposing tit-for-tat tariffs after talks broke down at the last moment in August.Trump has also threatened further tariffs on the EU if the associate membership plan proved "hostile" to the US, calling the idea laughable and labelling Canada a "terrible trading partner".Champagne said the trade war was not a conflict chosen by Canada."We responded because at some stage you have to say 'enough is enough'. No one can infringe on our economic sovereignty... the world took notice," he said.The minister said Canada did not seek escalation after its "measured, targeted and strategic... dollar-for-dollar, tariff-for-tariff" response and the country would "re-engage at the right time" with its southern neighbour. Affected industries would be supported "as long as it takes and whatever it takes", he added.Champagne argued that Canada's strong fiscal position helped underpin its resilience, and that the dispute with the US provided a "golden opportunity" to diversify. This is the backdrop to the promise of an "alliance of the future" between Canada and the EU, and the idea of "teaming up" with the UK too.Burnham will meet Trump for the first time this week, in New York at the UN General Assembly.Last year, after his election, Carney invited King Charles to open the Canadian Parliament in Ottawa, a move widely seen as a rebuff to Trump's repeated suggestion that Commonwealth Canada could become part of the US.The detail of the offer made by the EU to negotiate "associate membership" for Canada is yet to be formalised.Champagne said this was "a moment of great opportunities" and to strengthen the existing relationship between Canada and the EU.Carney last week pointed to Canadian membership of EU university, scientific research, AI and defence funding schemes, as well as for young Canadians and Europeans to "cross the ocean and be able to study and live".He said Canada could supply critical minerals and gas and would seek access to European advanced technologies.It is understood that both Canada and the EU see the opportunity for a process for like-minded nations which might not ever be full members, for example Australia.

schema.headline: UK should 'team up' with Canada in new Europe alliance, Canadian minister says

title: Newspaper headlines: 'Russia to test Nato pact' and 'Labour eye tax raid'
description: The Guardian reports that European intelligence officials have raised the possibility of an imminent test of Nato by Russia, external, quoting one off
body: The Guardian reports that European intelligence officials have raised the possibility of an imminent test of Nato by Russia, external, quoting one official as saying an attack could come in a matter of "months not years". The paper says the escalation fears come as the UN General Assembly convenes in New York later this week, and amid intensifying airstrikes on both sides of Russia's war on Ukraine.The lead for the Sun is its own investigation made in conjunction with Channel 5 into the murder convictions of the neo-natal nurse Lucy Letby, who was found guilty of killing seven babies and attempting to kill seven more. The paper says it has spoken to a "top consultant" who worked alongside her, who claims that she may have been a scapegoat to cover up, external for failings at the Countess of Chester Hospital. One mother tells the paper that her baby died six months after Letby had been moved off the neo-natal unit.The Times says it's carried out analysis which shows that more than half of Labour MPs in England and Wales have a higher number of people claiming disability benefit in their constituencies than the size of their majorities. The paper says the figures highlight what it calls the "political peril", external facing ministers trying to cut the welfare bill.Labour is considering raising Capital Gains Tax, external to help fund an increase to the income tax personal allowance, according to the Daily Telegraph. It says the idea has come from the Labour donor Dale Vince, who has warned the party that wealth is being "taxed more lightly than work". The paper also quotes the green energy entrepreneur as saying that the move would give "millions of people a meaningful boost" - with the biggest benefit going to those on the lowest incomes.The Daily Mail reports that Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch would ditch what it's calling a "tourist tax, external" which visitors to the UK have to pay on goods. The paper says she is pledging to bring back the VAT-free shopping initiative which was axed by her party in 2021. Speaking to the Mail, Badenoch said Britain should be a "magnet" for tourists who want to spend.

schema.headline: Newspaper headlines: 'Russia to test Nato pact' and 'Labour eye tax raid'

title: Young people are not snowflakes, head of mental health review says
description: Accusations that the young are a snowflake generation are wrong, the head of an independent review into mental health, ADHD and autism has told the BB
body: Accusations that the young are a snowflake generation are wrong, the head of an independent review into mental health, ADHD and autism has told the BBC.Prof Peter Fonagy said in an exclusive interview that there had been a real rise in mental distress among children and young people, with anxiety, depression, self-harm and eating disorders the most common.He said it was "harder to be young" now given the economic and employment uncertainty young people face, coupled with the challenges presented by social media.His review was ordered nine months ago by Wes Streeting after the then-health secretary claimed in an interview that young people were over-diagnosed and "written off".It is likely to feed into government policies on everything from NHS services and benefits to support for young people who are not in education, employment or training.Fonagy said he chose to speak to the BBC ahead of the publication, which is expected later this week, because he was concerned the debate around ADHD and autism would "obscure" the wider issue of mental health.More than 100 experts and families with experience of mental health problems have worked on the review with Fonagy, a clinical psychologist and adviser to NHS England.He said it will conclude that the rise in mental health problems since the 1990s was real, with about one in four 16 to 24-year-olds now struggling.The data on this is contested as some sources rely on self-reporting, while sceptics argue greater awareness and reduced stigma around mental health mean more people are coming forward.Some have also questioned whether society was now over-medicalising distress in people's lives – giving people diagnoses when what they are facing is temporary stress that they should learn to cope with.Last year, the BBC found that many GPs had concerns about over-diagnosis and felt normal life stresses were being over-medicalised.NHS figures, external show the number of children and young people in contact with mental health services in England has risen by 50% in the past five years.Fonagy said his personal battle with mental health when he was young was a driving factor in his desire to help young people.He experienced suicidal thoughts as a teenager after moving to London from Hungary without his parents. But he says he was fortunate to get therapy from a local service that "saved his life"."It's harder to be young now," the 74-year-old said, adding that his review "dismisses the idea of a snowflake generation"."I'm in awe of the way they have adjusted to an environment that is far more difficult than I ever had to face."He said economic and employment uncertainty, as well as the pressures of social media, had created a "very toxic" environment for young people."They are a generation that has real serious challenges that I would not wish to have had when I was their age."Adults have let them down. We're the first generation that probably collectively feels we had a better life than our children will have."So, to the person who says it's a snowflake generation, just try living 24 hours as a 16-year-old."Young people the BBC spoke to who have struggled with their mental health say it is important that the government acts on the findings of Fonagy's report when it comes out."It's all very well having this flashy report, but it's useless if they don't put that into practice," Omari, 22, said.He had a tough time at school, but said his teachers did not listen. "I made an attempt on my life because I was really struggling with bullying. I was 15."Suddenly, when I did end up in hospital, they all wanted to care. But it's like you're a bit too little, too late here."Others expressed concern about their futures. Mattea, 17, is in temporary social housing and has struggled with anxiety and depression."I don't know what's going to happen to my life," she said, adding that she felt like adults had let her down."No one's going to come and sort my life out for me. I have to do it on my own."Fonagy said the support being provided to young people needed to be improved.The NHS, he said, was simply "not fit for purpose".He said too many people were being left on waiting lists, pointing to figures that show one in three people referred to mental health services were still waiting for help after a year.There were some positives steps being taken, he said, including the rollout of mental health teams to work closely with schools.However, he said tackling the problem will require action across society – in education, employment, housing and families themselves.For example, Fonagy blamed cuts in youth services over the past decade or so for leading to fewer places for young people to mix and develop a sense of belonging."We need to have opportunities for them to participate, because participating in things... maintains good mental health."He also said it was striking that loneliness among young people had increased since 2000, linking it to the rise in use of phones and social media, which have reduced face-to-face contact and disrupted sleep patterns, both of which are damaging to mental health.But as well as addressing phone use, he said there were other things families and friends could do."Saying to someone, 'I notice you're not quite the same as yesterday. Is there anything the matter?' Knowing there is someone who knows makes an enormous difference."His hope? That working together, society can make a difference. "I want young people to hear that when they feel anxious, depressed or distressed, that it's a real problem, but a problem we can do something about."When I needed help, I got it. I want everyone to have that chance."

schema.headline: Young people are not snowflakes, head of mental health review says

title: England and Wales to have specialist courts for rape cases
description: Specialist courts to handle cases of rape and other sexual offences will be introduced across England and Wales over the next two years, the prime min
body: Specialist courts to handle cases of rape and other sexual offences will be introduced across England and Wales over the next two years, the prime minister has announced.Each crown court will have at least one courtroom set up to hear such cases, while alleged victims will be able to view proceedings remotely and give evidence from a separate room via video link.They will also be provided with private entrances and waiting rooms to separate them from defendants, though this will be dependent on the architecture of each building.Rape Crisis England and Wales said this was a "significant step forward" that would introduce several reforms it had been requesting for years."Taken together, they reflect the urgency of ensuring that courts are fit for purpose and properly meet the needs of victims and survivors, which is crucial to securing justice," the charity's chief executive, Ciara Bergman, said.Charities have complained that low prosecution rates for sexual offences and delays to court proceedings had disuaded victims from coming forward or pursuing justice.Just 2.8% of rape offences recorded by police led to prosecutions in the year ending March 2024 and were the crimes that took the longest to investigate.A prior ONS study suggested that only a sixth of the actual number of rape and attempted rape victims had reported their assault to the police, with more than a third saying this was because they felt the police could not help or that the process would be humiliating.Victims minister Alex Davies-Jones said the new measures were part of efforts to "get to grips" with a backlog of Crown Court cases, which stood at 80,098 at the end of March.RapeCrisis England and Wales said 15,373 of these cases - 19% - related to sexual offences.Davies-Jones told BBC Breakfast that the introduction of specialist courtrooms "isn't enough on its own" to tackle the backlog and stressed the importance of the Courts and Tribunals Bill to improve "timeliness, effectiveness and also prevention". The Conservatives say the "long overdue" move should not come with restricting the number of jury trials, which is another provision of the bill.Under the new measures, expected to cost around £23m of the Ministry of Justice's budget, court staff will also be given "trauma-informed training" and a single person of contact will be assigned to each survivor.From next month, trials will be given a fixed date rather than placed on floating lists in what Prime Minister Andy Burnham said was an effort to "rebalance the scales of justice and put victims first".There are 84 crown court buildings across England and Wales, containing around 500 courtrooms, and Davies-Jones said the government was determined that every one of them would have at least one specialist rape and sexual offences courtroom by 2028.Where architecture might prevent courtroom upgrades, Davies-Jones said staff would be expected to co-ordinate a "trauma informed approach" - for instance by scheduling different arrival times and rooms to give evidence from for victims and defendants.The government said the changes follow Labour MP Charlotte Nichols showing "immense strength and bravery" in speaking publicly about being raped and calling for changes to the justice system.Nichols waived her automatic right to anonymity in March when she made a Commons speech in which she described having to wait more than 1,000 days to go to court.Earlier this year, the government announced that rape victims would be given access to specialist legal advice throughout the criminal justice process.Labour promised in its 2024 manifesto to halve violence against women and girls within a decade."For too long, victims of rape and serious sexual offences have felt let down by our justice system," Burnham said. "Prosecution rates for rape remain shamefully low, with many victims waiting years for justice. This is not good enough."Nichols accused the then-Justice Secretary David Lammy of using victims as a "cudgel" to push through his reforms of the legal system when she spoke publicly for the first time about being raped.She was criticising the Courts and Tribunals Bill's plans to limit jury trials to cases with a likely prison sentence of three years or more.Nichols said she had waited 1,088 days to go to court, with every day being "agony". Her attacker, she said, was acquitted at crown court but subsequently ordered to pay compensation after she won a civil case against him."It is because I have endured every indignity that our broken criminal justice system could mete out that I care what kind of reform will actually deliver justice for survivors and victims of crime more widely," she said.The Conservatives said in response to news of the specialist courts roll-out that tackling delays to criminal rape trials was "long overdue", while pushing Labour to commit to scrapping plans to restrict jury trials. "The fact that victims have been withdrawing their cases because they have taken too long has been a disgrace," said shadow justice secretary Nick Timothy.  "Labour need to get courts sitting throughout the year, end the delays and clear the backlog – not undermine our right to a trial by jury."Last year, the Salford Survivor Project charity said victims of rape and sexual assault were being "failed by the system" as court backlogs reached a record high.The long delays for cases to go to trial were having a serious impact on victims' mental health, it said.A few months later, a woman who says she was sexually assaulted by a taxi driver on her 21st birthday told BBC News she had dropped the case because of court delays.She reported the alleged incident in early 2022 and gave evidence in court in December 2023, but the case was adjourned until September 2024 when the judge fell ill."I couldn't let this hurt me further," she said.If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, information and support can be found at the BBC's Action Line website.

schema.headline: England and Wales to have specialist courts for rape cases

title: Sri Lanka's Chemmani mass grave reopens wounds from the civil war - and families want answers
description: Workers came across human remains – and unearthed a mass grave of 572 peopleImage source, Ranjan Arun Prasadh, BBCImage caption, Jeyaruby Jeyabalan wa
body: Workers came across human remains – and unearthed a mass grave of 572 peopleImage source, Ranjan Arun Prasadh, BBCImage caption, Jeyaruby Jeyabalan was 12 when her father, Kandaiah Jayapalan, disappearedByAnbarasan EthirajanGlobal Affairs CorrespondentWhen a mass grave was unearthed in northern Sri Lanka last February, it was not by design. Workers were digging to extend a cremation ground in the Chemmani area of the Jaffna region when they suddenly discovered human remains, prompting an investigation. By August, archaeologists had completed the third phase of the excavation at the site, during which they found the skeletal remains of 572 people, including children and infants.Among the dead were artefacts from their lives – bangles, a school bag, a milk bottle.It is believed to be the largest mass grave site ever uncovered in Sri Lanka. There had been whispers of its existence before - a soldier on trial for the rape and murder of a young woman during the country's devastating civil war, had spoken about a mass grave which contained hundreds of bodies. Rights groups said they were disappeared civiliansBut there was no proof - until now.  And while the discovery is devastating, it has offered hope to people like Jeyaruby Jeyabalan, whose father was among thousands of people who disappeared during the decades-long war. Jeyabalan and families like his hope that answers about what happened to their loved ones lie among the bodies.Many Tamils believe the grave holds the victims of extrajudicial killings carried out during the civil war. They are calling for an investigation – and for justice.But the excavation process at Chemmani has moved slowly, testing the patience of families searching for answers about their disappeared loved ones. The discovery of hundreds of remains near a previously identified mass grave has fuelled anger among the Tamils, who have long-demanded a thorough inquiry into disappearances. Many fear the mass grave will eventually fade from public attention because of a lack of political will to pursue the truth – and so the grave has become a rallying point for renewed protests in Sri Lanka's north.Two decades waiting for answersSri Lanka, particularly the Tamil-dominated north and east, suffered decades of conflict. The war, which lasted from 1983 to 2009, divided the island-nation along ethnic lines. Tamil Tiger rebels fought for an independent state in the north-east of the country due to what they called systematic discrimination by the Sinhalese-dominated government.The conflict lasted 26 years and the fighting killed an estimated 100,000 people. It also left about 23,000 – mostly Tamils – missing.Both the security forces and Tamil Tigers are accused of atrocities and crimes.Image source, Kumanan Kanapathippillai, BBCImage caption, A baby's bottle was among the personal items uncovered at the grave site.In 1995, after a bloody conflict, the Sri Lankan army wrested control of the Jaffna Peninsula from the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE). It was seen as a key turning point in the war, which ended with the defeat of the Tigers in 2009. As they extended control in the late 1990s, the entire Chemmani region became part of a high-security zone and was dotted with army camps, check points and security posts. There was an army camp in Chemmani close to the cemetery as well.Some at that time described the Jaffna region as an "open prison" - and the security forces were accused of causing the disappearance of thousands of civilians, something Sri Lankan governments have always denied. "I was 12 years old when my father was picked up by the Sri Lankan army at a checkpoint close to Chemmani area in September 1996. We still don't know what happened to him," Jeyaruby Jayapalan, who now lives in Jaffna, tells the BBC.She recalls how, after learning of his disappearance, the family panicked and visited military camps and police stations across Jaffna in a desperate search for information without any luck. He never came back.Her father, Kandaiah Jayapalan, was a government employee who also ran a roadside café not far from Chemmani."I went to Chemmani mass grave with many others hoping that I will find some answers. But we didn't find any material evidence. We want a detailed forensic analysis of the human remains," says Jeyaruby.Two weeks before Kandaiah Jayapalan vanished, an 18-year-old Tamil school girl, Krishanthi Kumaraswamy, disappeared in the same area.In 1998, a court in Colombo sentenced five soldiers to death for the rape and murder of Kumaraswamy and for killing three of her family members. The case drew global attention at that time. Their bodies were later found buried in Chemmani area.It is among the most infamous cases from the conflict – and the grave currently under investigation is within 100 metres of the remains of Kumaraswamy and others were found. In a startling court testimony, one of the convicted soldiers, Somaratne Rajapakse, alleged that between 300 and 400 people who had been killed in the mid-1990s were buried in Chemmani.His claim led to the first excavation at Chemmani a year later, during which investigators unearthed more than 10 human skeletons. Human rights activists believed those remains were linked to people who had disappeared during the civil war, but there was little judicial follow-up.Activists say that because the war with the Tamil rebels was ongoing, the then government didn't pursue the investigation and did not explain why. The discovery of another mass grave in the same area has revived calls for accountability.Image caption, Map of Sri Lanka showing location of Chemmani "Preliminary inspections suggest this was not a normal burial site and not consistent with ordinary Hindu burial practices," says Gehan Gunatilleke, a commissioner with Human Rights Commission of Sri Lanka, which conducted inspections at Chemmani last year.Activists and experts say that while a few dozen bodies appeared to have been formally buried, the vast majority told a different story.Most of the human remains were found without clothing, packed tightly together and, in some cases, stacked on top of others. The graves were shallow, with bodies buried just one to two metres below the surface."There is a reasonable likelihood that the burials were unlawful and pursuant to extrajudicial killings," the Human Rights Commission of Sri Lanka said in a report last year.Past investigations haven't led to prosecutionsThe families of those disappeared during the conflict have responded to the discovery by holding protest meetings and remembrance ceremonies.Among them is Suseela, a 65-year-old woman who is looking for her son, Gnanaseelan Ravi, who was picked up by the Sri Lankan military in 2007, when he was 24."He was my only son, and I keep crying every day remembering him. My life is empty without him," she tells the BBC.She went to Chemmani grave but couldn't find any evidence, such as clothes or personal jewellery, that suggested her son was buried there.  DNA tests on the human remains are yet to be carried out.All the remains recovered so far from Chemmani have been kept in the Forensic Department of the University of Jaffna campus under court custody."We are preparing an interim report, and it will be submitted to the court by the end of September," Prof Raj Somadeva, the chief archaeologist of the mass grave told the BBC.Some of the samples are expected to be sent abroad for detailed examination to help determine the age of the remains. Separate medical analyses will be needed to establish the possible causes of death.More than 20 mass graves have been found across Sri Lanka in recent decades, but none have been conclusively linked to enforced disappearances or alleged extra-judicial killings in the north and south of the country – and none have led to prosecutions.Given the failure of the authorities to investigate previous mass graves, there is scepticism among many Tamil people over what the new investigation might achieve.They point out to the outcome of the investigation on another mass grave was unearthed in the north-western town of Mannar in 2018 in which more than 350 skeletal remains were found. Investigations proved inconclusive, leaving many families disappointed.They want Sri Lanka to be referred to the International Criminal Court.The government of President Anura Kumara Dissanayake insists that it is fully cooperating with the investigation.Image source, Kumanan Kanapathippillai, BBCImage caption, Suseela holds a photograph of her son, Gnanaseelan Ravi, who was picked up by the Sri Lankan military in 2007, when he was 24.After coming to power in September 2024, Dissanayake promised to work towards justice and ethnic reconciliation. But his government vehemently opposes any international mechanism to investigate alleged war crimes committed during the ethnic conflict, disappointing Tamils."We will continue with the excavation work at Chemmani," Harshana Nanayakkara, Sri Lanka's justice minister told the BBC."We need to analyse the skeletons and find out how these people died. Then we have to carry out DNA tests," he said.The government, he insists, has also asked the families to give their DNA so that it can be analysed later with the remains.During his inspection at Chemmani in June, the minister promised investigations to find justice and truth to bring an end to the matter. He also promised that necessary funding will be allocated for the excavation.The Sri Lankan army spokesman, Brigadier Waruna Gamage rejects allegations that security forces buried civilians after massacring them."All the allegations should be proved in court," he told the BBC.Calls for international assistanceImage source, Kumanan Kanapathippillai, BBCImage caption, Families of the disappeared are protesting, demanding international investigation into Chemmani mass grave.The delays in investigating past crimes have attracted stringent criticism from rights groups.After years of international pressure, in 2018 the government set up an independent body, the Office of the Missing Persons (OMP), to investigate the disappearances. But those affected say it hasn't made much progress in finding their missing relatives."Many cases of forced disappearance, torture and killing remain stalled, while families of victims and human rights defenders face threats and intimidation," Human Rights Watch said in a report earlier this month.The United Nations has urged Sri Lanka to seek international help in identifying the victims, to find out how they died, and who is responsible."This is a situation where victims are deeply frustrated, have lived with pain for decades, have come to distrust past investigations," Rory Mungoven, the Asia-Pacific chief at the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights tells the BBC."I think involving international assistance would help to bolster confidence in these investigations," he points out.Successive Sri Lankan governments have strongly resisted calls for international investigations into alleged wartime atrocities.During earlier reporting trips to Sri Lanka, I met parents and family members of the disappeared who campaigned for decades to the search for truth. Some have since passed away without ever discovering the fates of their loved ones.Human rights groups say that President Dissanayake's government now has an opportunity to break from a long-standing pattern of delay and denial and deliver accountability for grave abuses committed during the conflict.Suseela is determined to know the truth. "I don't know how long I will live with such uncertainty, but I want closure," she says.Additional Reporting by: Ranjan Arun Prasadh, BBC Tamil Service in Kandy and Kumanan Kanapathippillai in Jaffna.

schema.headline: Sri Lanka's Chemmani mass grave reopens wounds from the civil war - and families want answers

title: Union calls for halt to graded Ofsted inspections over health concerns
description: England's biggest school leaders' union has called for a halt to graded Ofsted inspections, saying they could pose a "risk to life" for school staff.T
body: England's biggest school leaders' union has called for a halt to graded Ofsted inspections, saying they could pose a "risk to life" for school staff.The National Association of Head Teachers (NAHT) said the change to inspections, rolled out nationally just under a year ago, had been severely harmful to school leaders' welfare.It said schools should instead be rated using short narrative reports that set out their strengths and areas they could improve.Ofsted said it had worked closely with unions and parents to develop the new report card inspection system and that it would continue to grade schools.Ofsted, England's schools inspectorate, introduced the report card system to replace its previous one or two-word judgements last November, following the death of head teacher Ruth Perry, who took her own life after Ofsted downgraded her school from "outstanding" to "inadequate".An inquest ruled that an Ofsted inspection had contributed to her death in January 2023.That led to a change in how Ofsted assessed schools, bringing in report cards designed to grade schools on several areas, rather than focusing on one overall grade.But the new system has faced criticism since it was first proposed, with Perry's sister Prof Julia Waters saying it appeared to be "a rehash of the discredited and dangerous system it is meant to replace".The NAHT issued a claim in the High Court for a judicial review over the changes, arguing there had not been adequate consultation on the new report cards before they were introduced, but this was rejected.Nearly a year after it was fully rolled out, the NAHT said evidence from its members suggested the new system is having a detrimental impact on school leaders' mental health.Testimonies seen by the BBC suggest head teachers are being left "overwhelmed" and "anxious", with the pressure caused by the inspections described as "intolerable".Although the system had been changed with the intention of lowering the burden on school leaders, the testimonies say the inspection and assessment process had become "higher stakes than ever before".Amanda Hulme, head teacher at Claypool Primary School in Bolton, said a recent inspection at her school had been "easily the most stressful experience" of her career."It was definitely damaging to my health and really quite distressing," she said."I couldn't sleep and it led to my blood pressure and pulse rate increasing."The effect on my team has also been significant, with some colleagues no longer wanting to pursue headship and another teacher considering leaving the profession entirely."The NAHT said it had shared examples of some of the "damaging experiences" it said its members had faced with Education Secretary Lucy Powell.Powell told LBC earlier this month that she took head teacher wellbeing "incredibly seriously" and that the system of accountability needed to be "supportive and understanding."I'll continue the work that I do with head teachers, head teacher representatives and others to make sure that we get this Ofsted framework, but also the culture and the whole regime, right," she said.The NAHT said the results of a recent survey of its members suggested that the majority who responded felt that inspections had worsened in the past 12 months.The union is now calling for inspections to pause to allow for a "fundamental review of how inspection works", drawing on examples from other nations.In Wales, the inspectorate Estyn has removed judgements such as "excellent" and "good" from its reports, instead summarising findings by highlighting a school's strengths and areas for improvement.Northern Ireland's Education and Training Inspectorate (ETI) also uses narrative reports without grades. Scotland's His Majesty's Inspectorate of Education (HIME) does use grades, but there has been a recent consultation on their use.NAHT general secretary Paul Whiteman said: "The clear theme emerging across all the feedback we have received is that this Ofsted framework is even more stressful than the one that preceded it."It poses a real and present danger to the well-being and mental health of school leaders and teachers, possibly even a risk to life."He said he welcomed the new education secretary's focus on teacher wellbeing, adding: "Really fundamental changes to inspection are needed, and we stand ready to work with the new government to achieve that."Ofsted said it had worked closely with teaching unions over the past three years to deliver significant reforms and reduce unnecessary pressure on teachers."Ofsted exists to raise standards for children and to provide clear reporting to parents," a spokesperson said."We will continue to engage closely with trades unions – but we will also continue to grade schools."

schema.headline: Union calls for halt to graded Ofsted inspections over health concerns

title: Spygate: Southampton and Tonda Eckert await FA ruling
description: "I would lie if I say that the summer has just been easy. Of course, if you care deeply about your profession, about the football club, there's nothin
body: "I would lie if I say that the summer has just been easy. Of course, if you care deeply about your profession, about the football club, there's nothing that prepares you for that. There just isn't."Eckert speaks slowly and with an intense gaze when asked to reflect on being at the centre of one of the biggest controversies in English football history.The 33-year-old apologised in June after an EFL independent disciplinary commission found he had orchestrated a "contrived and determined plan" to spy on Oxford United, Ipswich Town, then Middlesbrough before the play-off semi-final.Having insisted he was unaware it breached EFL rules, and that the spying had no impact on performances, Eckert was backed by Southampton.His team have made an encouraging start to the new season. Without the four-point deduction, they would be fourth in the table, rather than 13th."We've talked a lot over the summer of how we want to go through that process of addressing everything, giving everyone the chance to put questions out that are still there, to put out what they feel and have gone through, and then also close the door and move on," he says. "Because the reality is it's a new season. We have big ambitions as a football club, and in order to reach them, we need to move on."That is easier said than done, with Eckert in limbo while he awaits the outcome of the FA's disciplinary process."I've had the chance to sit down and just talk the FA through everything that happened," he says. "And now it's up to them to make a decision. I don't really have any emotions towards that."So does he feel the FA has listened to him during its investigation? "That was my impression," he says. "We sat for almost four hours, so it's been quite a long conversation."When asked whether he feels the club has been punished enough, and if a suspension for him would be excessive, Eckert chooses his words carefully."It's been a big, big punishment," he says. "Absolutely unheard of in the history of sports."And it's tough for me to say that because it concerns me. I'm judging on myself, not an outside situation. But I've asked for forgiveness for what I've done. I've apologised publicly."I think the punishment has been very hard on the club for the last season. And to go into a new season on minus four. And the rest is not for me to decide."Parsons is more forthright on whether the club has been punished enough."We don't know what the FA will actually hand out," he says. "It could be a long ban. It could be a short ban. It could be a suspended sentence."What we hope as a club is they actually recognise where we are at the moment, and what we've already been through, because I think it has to be taken into account. I really feel like we've taken enough. We've been hurt. I think it's one of the largest sanctions ever when it comes to football, or even sporting, history."This isn't just about the club, this is about people. We lose money not being in the Premier League, but [local] businesses lose money. We had to spend a huge amount on legal fees, and it really impacts the club even further. We don't want to be seen as a victim of this. We need to get on. We've had our cards dealt."When it is put to Parsons that the EFL's punishments applied to the club - rather than Eckert himself - he says: "I think it's impossible to sanction the manager without the club getting hurt even more."The most recent precedent for this case came at the 2024 Olympics women's tournament, when Fifa banned Bev Priestman - Canada's head coach - from all football for a year, after opponents New Zealand were spied on. Parsons insists "the Canadian case is very different" but if Eckert , who is only contracted until the end of the season, is also banned, how long would it have to be for the club to look elsewhere for a new coach?"We don't know," he says, firmly denying having approached other coaches in case Eckert has to leave. Parsons also says the club may appeal if the ruling goes against them."We can't worry about something we can't control at the moment," he says. "We have to deal with it when we get there but we're hoping that they look at it sensibly."Parsons says the club's ownership "want" to back Eckert."We've been through an entire transfer window when it comes to recruiting players for Tonda, and that's another challenge."We have to be looking at all scenarios. We've always spoken about any punishment being disproportionate...You're looking for fairness in approach. And have we had that treatment to us, from a disproportionate punishment? Well, I think a lot of people will view it that way. But do we want to sit there moaning about it? No."But it's going to be really tough to take if we get another punishment, on top of being thrown out of the play-offs, four points this season, and potentially more. So we're really hoping that the FA, the panel, are looking as this with a balanced view to what's already happened, because it's been really heavy."When compared to the £10m fines that both the FA and Premier League handed Chelsea this year for making £47m in secret payments related to transfers across several seasons when they were owned by Roman Abramovich, some would agree Southampton have suffered enough.Others however, would say the FA has little choice but to sanction Eckert.After all, according to the EFL commission, the club employed "a particularly deplorable approach" by using junior members of staff to conduct the spying "at the direction of senior personnel".An arbitration panel then detailed how a junior analyst intern said he felt under "extreme pressure". Southampton's initial response to the crisis also contained "inaccuracies". Middlesbrough's head of football Kieran Scott said the club's behaviour had been "disgusting"., external Parsons shrugs off such criticism. And when it is put to him that many expected Southampton to sack Eckert, and had they done so they would not be facing the current uncertainty, he replies: "Yeah, but Tonda also picked up the team in around 20th place in the Championship, and without him and his team we wouldn't have been in the play-off positions, and I think that deserves a bit of loyalty."OK, he has made a mistake and he's paid for that dearly. This has been really tough for him as a person already. I admire how strong he's been through this process because a lot of people could have cracked, the amount of pressure he was under."For his part, Eckert says he is "very grateful for the support of the club because that could have been very different, and I think in most cases would have been very different".The vast majority of Southampton fans that BBC Sport spoke to also seem to fully back the manager, something he says "means everything" to him.Another to be supported is the intern involved - Will Salt - who was recently handed a permanent role as an analyst in the club's academy. The scandal began when a photograph was published of Salt secretly filming Boro from behind a tree at their training ground before the play-off semi-final."He's been through a tough time," says Parsons. "When your photo is put out to the public, that is something tough to deal with. A lot of people probably underestimated how that could have impacted a young lad so we've got a job to make sure that he's looked after in his early career. But he's a talented boy as well. I get good feedback and he's got a good role at the club."Asked if reintegrating Salt had been challenging, given his allegations about the way he was treated, Parsons says: "I don't think Will said he felt under pressure directly from Tonda himself. He felt under pressure in the situation. And everybody knows in a job you can feel under pressure. "But, yeah, I think Will's managed himself really well, and he'll grow from this."So has the club learned its lessons? Parsons insists Eckert has studied the EFL's regulations, but also argues the rules could be clearer. "They're very grey - that's something I'll continue to raise in EFL meetings," he says."But look, we've done something wrong, we'll get on with it."Moving on is not easy, though. Last week, Wrexham's owners aimed a dig at Southampton by referencing the scandal in a social media advert before the two teams met. And during matches, rival fans regularly remind the club of the scandal."History is history and it'll be a part of our story going forwards," says Parsons. "It's about how we react now. It's given us a real togetherness and hopefully that continues through the season because we're stronger like that anyway. "There's a bit of siege mentality as well, right - of 'everybody's against us', so we've got to embrace it."The Championship has now paused until next month for the international break. By the time Southampton next play - against local rivals Portsmouth on 11 October - Eckert should have learned his fate.For now, however, his future remains uncertain.

schema.headline: Spygate: Southampton and Tonda Eckert await FA ruling

title: Quadruple amputee from Oxford enters the Big Brother house
description: Charlotte Nott has never let anything hold her back.The student, from Oxford, is a quadruple amputee, having lost the lower parts of her arms and legs
body: Charlotte Nott has never let anything hold her back.The student, from Oxford, is a quadruple amputee, having lost the lower parts of her arms and legs to meningitis when she was just two years old.Now 18, Charlotte is a contestant in the latest series of Big Brother, something she has dreamed about for most of her life.Her dad, Alex, told BBC Radio Oxford he was anxious about her appearance on the show, but said there had never been much point telling his daughter not to do something she had her sights on. That resilience was on full display within seconds of Charlotte's arrival on the show. During the launch, her shoe broke as she stepped out to be introduced, and she had to remove her prosthetic legs on stage before entering the house."Maybe it was my fate to walk in with no legs," she told the diary room. "Maybe that was just what was meant to happen."She added that she was used to going without her prosthetics at home. "When I'm at home, I have my legs off all the time," she said. "When I'm cooking, I have my legs off. I like to be four foot. I like to be tiny, like a little tiny doll."Alex said the moment had summed up his daughter's unstoppable nature perfectly."People are surprised at anything I do, even normal things like cooking, doing my makeup, getting dressed," she said. "They're probably going to be surprised at the most normal things for me."Asked what she would do with the prize money if she won, Charlotte said her prosthetic legs cost around £25,000 each."I probably would put a lot of it into savings," she said. "My prosthetic legs are about £25,000 per leg, so probably put half in savings and then the other half... just go on a nice holiday, just kind of spend it."Caroline Hughes, senior support services Manager for Meningitis Research Foundation, said the long term consequences of the disease "remain widely misunderstood"."Every day, we support people navigating the physical, emotional and practical challenges that can follow a meningitis diagnosis," she said."That's why it is so powerful to see people like Charlotte sharing their experience on a platform like Big Brother. "By speaking so openly about her story, she is helping bring greater understanding of the long-term impact meningitis can have, while also enabling others affected by the disease to feel seen, heard and less alone."The 23rd series of Big Brother began on 13 September and will last 54 days, making it the longest series since 2017.ITV said the series had been "reimagined as a house of surprises" and viewers could expect "ambitious tasks, high-stakes nominations and dramatic live evictions".

schema.headline: Quadruple amputee from Oxford enters the Big Brother house

title: Key takeaways from BBC interview as Earl Spencer defends claims about King
description: Figure caption, Watch: Earl Spencer says he's 'telling the truth' about what Charles said after Diana diedByAndré Rhoden-Paul Earl Spencer has told th
body: Figure caption, Watch: Earl Spencer says he's 'telling the truth' about what Charles said after Diana diedByAndré Rhoden-Paul Earl Spencer has told the BBC writing his book about sister Princess Diana, which has made headlines for its criticism of King Charles, was his "duty...as an eyewitness to history".In an interview with the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg ahead of the memoir's release on Tuesday, Earl Spencer said he wanted "to put things down once and for all that were true".Among claims made in Swan Song about the King, who was then the Prince of Wales, was that he said "we'll forget her soon enough" during an argument over whether Princes William and Harry should walk in Diana's funeral procession.In a strongly worded response, Buckingham Palace said the King was "mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgement and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss".Here are the key moments from Earl Spencer's interview, which include his first account of how he was told about Diana's death and criticism of press coverage of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex. Earl initially told Diana's crash was 'not too serious'Earl Spencer was in South Africa when Princess Diana died in a Paris car crash in the early hours of 31 August 1997, along with close friend Dodi Fayed and the driver of the car.He told the BBC he got a call in the middle of the night from his sister Lady Jane Fellowes, who said Princess Diana had been in a crash but "it's not too serious". But then he "kept getting more and more distressing calls" from his sister. "And then my sister Jane said, 'I'm afraid she's died.' It started... as a little prang, and then it became a broken leg, perhaps a head injury, and then death."Charles had 'giddy tone' after Diana's deathFigure caption, Earl Spencer describes 'giddy tone' in Charles' voice during call after Diana's deathDescribing the hours after her death, Earl Spencer said he took a call at his home in Cape Town from Prince Charles, who told him how he broke the news to Princes William and Harry at Balmoral Castle. "I felt there was a sort of giddy tone," he told the BBC. "I'd had a lot of calls that day from people who cared, who were stunned... and I just felt there was a lightness in his tone about Diana's death that really jarred with me."In his book, Earl Spencer compares his tone to like a "lottery winner" and says he suspects the prince's reaction was based on how this event would free him to marry the woman he loved, his future wife Queen Camilla. When asked by Kuenssberg if he could be sure that is what Prince Charles was thinking, Earl Spencer said: "I cannot be sure, I'm saying that's what I assume from the tone is a possibility." Earl Spencer told the BBC he had been discussing funeral arrangements with a palace official, who said it had been agreed Princes William and Harry should walk behind their mother's coffin. Unhappy, he said he told the official it is not what his sister would have wanted, before the conversation came to an end. Soon after, the earl says he took a call from Prince Charles, who asked him about his opposition to it. "I said, 'Well, of course not, sir, she wouldn't want it'. And then he said, 'Well, I walked behind Lord Mountbatten's coffin.' And I said, 'Yes, but you were 30 and he wasn't your mother'."He then claims Charles went "ballistic... and ranted for a while" about the Spencer's sense of duty not being adequate enough before "he said 'We'll forget her [Diana] soon enough'.""I really was so stunned and after a stunned silence I said 'I can not believe you just said that' and I hung up on him", the earl told Kuenssberg during his sit down interview at his Althorp estate. Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Princes William and Harry walked in the procession behind their mother's coffinResponding to the Palace's statement pushing back on the story, Earl Spencer said: "I can tell you here and now, those are exactly the words he said. "I've only ever had two calls on the line with Prince Charles at any stage in my life. "I was hyper-alert to what he was saying, and those are precisely the words he said. And I promise that to you now. Genuinely, that is what he said. "I don't hear him saying he didn't say that."The earl said he told "close friends and family" about the "monstrous" comment. When asked if people should believe him or the King, he said: "Well, I'm telling the truth... what else would have made me hang up on the King that day?"On what Princes William and Harry might think of the comments being brought up nearly 30 years later, he added the words "will not be a surprise" to the brothers.He also said his renowned funeral eulogy, in which he said his sister's qualities would never be "extinguished from our minds", was a "direct rebuttal" of the prince's comments. Princess Diana: My Sister's StoryWatch the full interview with Laura Kuenssberg.'I know lots of things about the King' not in the bookTalking about his motivations for writing the book, Earl Spencer, aged 62, said it was his "duty... as an eyewitness to history" and as someone in the "final season of my life" with his parents dying in their sixties."I'm aware of mortality and I wanted to just put things down once and for all that were true," the historian and journalist explained."This is not a threat, it's a fact, I know lots of things about the King which I chose not to include in the book because they were not relevant."When put to him that the  statement sounded like a threat when it involved potentially damaging information, he said: "No, not at all a threat, it's just the reality."Kuenssberg questioned why he included an account of a conversation in which his sister told him Prince Charles was in love with his valet - a claim Earl Spencer said was improbable - and asked if he was motivated in including some of these allegations to create interest to sell the book. "It's in the context of a conversation where Diana is telling me that her marriage is over," the earl replied."It's a brother's tribute, a loving tribute to a sister.  And I think she deserves honesty so that's what I've delivered."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Earl Spencer said he was concerned about security for Duke and Duchess of SussexEarl Spencer worries about Harry's lack of police protectionWhen asked about how he thinks Prince Harry has been treated by the Royal Family, Earl Spencer told the BBC he is reluctant to discuss it, but he said he was concerned about his security. "I would say that I personally worry about the fifth-in-line to the throne who's served in the military not having any police protection," he said. "As an uncle who's seen his sister die in very, very preventable circumstances, that I would veer towards protection."It is understood the committee that oversees royal and VIP security, known as Ravec, is to reconsider Prince Harry and Meghan's level of police protection now they and their two children are full-time residents in the UK rather than visitors.When asked about how the press treated Princess Diana and now Prince Harry and Meghan, he said tabloid articles "could be really really unpleasant". "It would really be beholden on people to learn from Diana's example. I'm not here to speak for Harry and Meghan, but for anyone who's being destroyed in this way daily, it must be such a cancerous influence in their life," Earl Spencer said. "[Diana] was really brought low by all that criticism. And yeah I suppose it's a pity when I see echoes of that now."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The earl said he hopes his nephews resolve their differences'I hope William and Harry resolve row' Earl Spencer said he did not take sides - as he perceives is the "perception in the media" - in the dispute between Princes William and Harry. "I'm on my deceased sister's sons' side, both of them. And if either of them wanted anything then I'd be equally there for them," he said. "And I never get involved in one camp or the other, except as a benign figure I hope."He said there are a "lot of reasons on both sides" why the brothers' relationship had "got to this stage". "I hope one day it's resolved, but I don't know all – I certainly don't know what's been done in the finer detail and so I would feel intrusive if I got more involved than to say of course a mother would want her two sons to be happy together and love each other," he said. Diana 'convinced she couldn't trust people' after Bashir interviewReflecting on the time before Princess Diana's death, Kuenssberg asked if the infamous BBC Panorama interview with journalist Martin Bashir in 1995 might have been linked indirectly to his sister finding herself in Paris in 1997. Shortly after the interview broadcast, in which Princess Diana admitted having an affair and said Prince Charles's affair with then-Camilla Parker Bowles made her feel worthless, the Queen wrote to Prince Charles and Princess Diana telling them to divorce.A 2021 inquiry found Bashir acted in a "deceitful" way  by mocking up fake bank statements - which falsely suggested individuals were being paid to keep Diana under surveillance - and showing them to Earl Spencer to gain access to the late princess.Earl Spencer said he did make "a connection" between the crash and the Panorama interview and said they conned both him and Diana."People said, 'Oh, she was paranoid'. She wasn't paranoid. She was convinced that she couldn't trust people because the evidence was there.  And, you know, I think that left her vulnerable that night."The BBC and Bashir apologised to King Charles, Earl Spencer and Princes William and Harry after the 2021 report was published.The BBC's then-director general, Tim Davie, said: "Although the report states that Diana, Princess of Wales, was keen on the idea of an interview with the BBC, it is clear that the process for securing the interview fell far short of what audiences have a right to expect. We are very sorry for this."Earl supports 'a modern monarchy'Earl Spencer, the ninth earl of an aristocratic family whose peerage dates back to the 18th Century and retains its vast estate, told the BBC he is "all for a monarchy, but I like a modern monarchy". Talking about the "jarring" protocol around the monarchy, he said: "You know, you mentioned the statement earlier, 'His Majesty says", I just don't think it's healthy for a human being to be seen in such archaic, servile terms."When Kuenssberg asked him if he supported this monarchy, following the damning book he has just written, he said: "I do."He added when challenged: "Well, I'm not dealing with King Charles as monarch in this book, this is all 30-odd years ago and what was said and done then."An emotional tribute to a sister he misses every dayFigure caption, Watch: 'You never get over it': Earl Spencer's emotional tribute to late sister DianaAs the interview came to an end, Earl Spencer was asked whether he would ever be able to get over his sister's death.Visibly emotional, he said he misses Diana "every day", adding "that's the thing with sibling loss, you never get over it."But his upcoming book, he said, is a way for him to have a final say on Diana's life before stepping off "into the sunset"."One of the reasons I called this Swan Song actually is because it's my sign off," he said."I have been Diana's brother, this is my final take on the situation… I'm not here to bang on about Diana, this is my final word, a celebration of her."
